title: Neutral components and translations for finite-type group schemes
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G/k$ be a group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A connected component means a maximal connected subset of the underlying space, where connectedness is as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]. The component $C$ containing the identity is open and closed. Equipped with its open subscheme structure [def-weil-open-immersion], it is a closed subgroup scheme of $G$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. There are finitely many connected components. For every connected component $D$, there is a point $g\in G(k)$ for which left translation $t_g:G\to G$, $x\mapsto gx$, restricts to an isomorphism of $k$-schemes $C\xrightarrow{\sim}D$, with $D$ also given its open subscheme structure. No reducedness, smoothness, affineness, properness or characteristic-zero hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0B7R, proposition-connected-component (canonical closed identity subgroup), finite-type case; Milne, literature/milne-algebraic-groups_iAG2017.pdf, Proposition 1.34, Corollary 1.35 and dimension discussion before Proposition 1.37, printed pp.16-18 (finite components and translations).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] to $G$: finite type includes locally finite type. Its $G^0$ is precisely the open subscheme $C$ on the identity component, is open and closed, and is a subgroup scheme. Its inclusion is also a closed immersion by [def-weil-closed-immersion]: on every open $V$ of $G$, restriction $\mathcal O_G(V)\to\mathcal O_C(V\cap C)$ is surjective, since a section on $V\cap C$ extends by zero on the disjoint open $V\setminus C$. Thus this is a closed subgroup with the stipulated open, not reduced, scheme structure.

source.place: Tag 0B7R, proposition-connected-component; finite-type assembly as in Milne, Algebraic Groups (2017), Proposition 1.34 and pp.16-18.

proof.text: Let $D$ be any connected component and choose $x\in D$. The closed subset $Z=\overline{\{x\}}$ is connected: every nonempty relatively open subset of $Z$ contains $x$, so two such opens cannot disconnect it. Moreover $D\cup Z$ is connected, since its two connected subsets meet at $x$; a separation would have to put both in the same part. Maximality of $D$ therefore gives $Z\subseteq D$. By [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], the closed points of $G$ in $Z$ are dense in the nonempty space $Z$, hence one exists, say $z$. By [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], the composite $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(z)\to G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an isomorphism. Composing its inverse with $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(z)\to G$ gives $g\in G(k)$ with image $z\in D$.

source.place: Tag 0478, lemma-locally-finite-type-Jacobson; Tag 01TB in morphisms.tex, lemma-jacobson-finite-type-points; elementary connectedness argument as in Topology Tag 004T.

proof.text: By [lem-sc-translation-automorphism], $t_g=L_g$ is an isomorphism with inverse $t_{g^{-1}}$; its definition is [def-sc-group-scheme-translate]. In particular $t_g(e)=g$. Its underlying homeomorphism carries $C$ to the component of $g$: the image is connected and contains $g$, and the inverse image of any larger connected subset would contradict maximality of $C$. Components meeting at $g$ agree, since their union is connected; hence $t_g(C)=D$. As $C$ is open, $D$ is open. Restrict $t_g$ and its inverse to these opens; the homeomorphisms and structure-sheaf isomorphisms restrict, so they are inverse isomorphisms of the open subschemes by [def-weil-open-immersion]. This proves the asserted scheme isomorphism, including nilpotents.

source.place: Section 1b, Proposition 1.34 and dimension discussion before Proposition 1.37, printed pp.16-18; translation homogeneity of 1.8.

proof.text: Connected components cover $G$: for a point $x$, the union of all connected subsets containing $x$ is connected (a separation would put every such subset in the part containing $x$), and is maximal. Distinct components are disjoint, since the union of two meeting connected subsets is connected. Step 3 makes this an open cover. By [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is quasi-compact, so $G$ is quasi-compact and this cover has a finite subcover. Every component is nonempty and disjoint from the others, so none can be omitted; the set of components is therefore finite.

source.place: Tag 004T, lemma-connected-components, parts (3)-(4); quasi-compactness applied to the component cover.
